articles.title: 2026 Clinical Catalog Enrichment: Node.js Speech-to-Text API Fallback When Whisper Is Unavailable
articles.excerpt: Short answer: Put a provider-neutral adapter in front of the speech-to-text API, classify why Whisper is unavailable, and send only normalized, reviewable text into catalog enrichment. A speech-to-tex…
articles.body: Short answer: Put a provider-neutral adapter in front of the speech-to-text API, classify why Whisper is unavailable, and send only normalized, reviewable text into catalog enrichment. A speech-to-text fallback in a healthtech catalog pipeline should protect the catalog's data contract, not pretend that every recognizer produces interchangeable text. My default design is a small transcription boundary: accept one job shape, normalize provider responses into one internal result, and route the same audio through an ordered set of adapters when a primary capability is unavailable. The enrichment stage then works from that normalized result and records uncertainty instead of silently inventing product attributes. The adapter is the product boundary.

articles.excerpt: AI can write a whole feature in minutes. You ask, it builds, the tests pass, and you click approve. But here's the problem: a lot of us now merge code we can't really explain. And when it breaks at 2…
articles.body: AI can write a whole feature in minutes. You ask, it builds, the tests pass, and you click approve. But here's the problem: a lot of us now merge code we can't really explain. And when it breaks at 2 AM, nobody on the team knows how it works. I saw this happen again and again, so I built Comprende , a free and open-source plugin for Claude Code. What does it do? Comprende has two parts. 1. Explain as you build While Claude writes code, it explains the important parts: new APIs you might not know tricky logic that isn't obvious risky stuff, like security or data loss It skips the boring parts, so you don't get a wall of text. It works for juniors and seniors: it looks at the code, not at your level. It also answers in your language.

articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady What I Built Picture a maintainer opening a repository to make one small change. Before reaching it, they notice an unused import, a README link pointing to a guide that moved, and an example command whose script no longer exists. None of those tasks is especially difficult. Each still asks for a context switch: locate the evidence, decide what the intended replacement was, edit the file, run checks, and work out whether anything else changed. The burden is in repeating the whole loop for work that rarely feels urgent enough to finish. PatchGardener turns that loop into a reviewable maintenance queue.

articles.body: Credit: Edgar Cervantes / Android Authority TL;DR YouTube has announced that it plans to roll out AV2 to the platform in early 2027. The AV2 codec will initially launch for the web version of YouTube. The company also hints at benefits for multi-view experiences. Earlier this year, the Alliance for Open Media released the definitive specs for the AV2 codec , which is expected to be about 25% to 32% more efficient than AV1. That means you get higher-quality streaming for the same bitrate or comparable quality at a lower bitrate. The benefit is that the codec can reduce the amount of bandwidth you’re consuming. YouTube is expected to adopt AV2, and it could arrive sooner than you would expect.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 24, 1946: V-2 rocket takes 1st photos of Earth from space
articles.excerpt: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. While these grainy, black-and-white images might not look like much today, they were a huge deal at the time, because no one had ever seen Earth from space before. The V-2 rocket launched from the White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico. It carried a 35-millimeter motion picture camera that captured a new frame every second and a half. The rocket soared to an altitude of about 65 miles before falling back to Earth. Both the rocket and the camera were destroyed after crashing into the Earth at a speed of about 340 miles per hour. But the film survived because it was protected inside a steel case. Scientists had to drive out into the New Mexico desert to retrieve the film.

articles.body: It didn’t take long for fans to figure out that the fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was going to be unlike any season of " Star Trek " before it. The entire season was one giant gimmick, and that gimmick was shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres. You could argue that an entire season of gimmick episodes is a bold risk: putting the characters in fun, wacky situations to see how they react. It could be interesting, but the season we got never made the most of the concept. It was all so safe and paint-by-numbers, and, most importantly, it didn't have anything profound or interesting to say. That should trouble any Trekkie.

To celebrate, we've put together a list of five Halloween-themed skywatching targets that you can enjoy with nothing but the naked eye or binoculars and, of course, clear skies. Over millennia, the night sky has helped shape human beliefs. In return, we have imprinted our myths, stories and perceptions upon it, seeing monsters and mythology in the twinkling lights of the stars and assigning sinister aspects to innocent cosmic objects. Many of these ghostly impressions and meanings have survived to the present day. Here are a few of our favorites. The Pleiades open star cluster Don't be fooled by their beauty; the blue-white stars of the Pleiades are dripping in spooky lore.

articles.title: SpaceX launches Starlink satellites from California as Falcon 9 cadence slows (video)
articles.excerpt: SpaceX sent 27 more of its Starlink broadband satellites to orbit today (Oct. 23), in its first Starlink launch in 11 days.
articles.body: SpaceX launched its newest batch of Starlink broadband internet satellites today (Oct. 23) from the California coast. The spacecraft, Starlink Group 15-15, were stacked 27 high inside the payload fairing of a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket , which lifted off from Pad 4E at Vandenberg Space Force Base at 6:48 p.m. EDT (2248 GMT; 3:48 p.m. local time in California). The rocket's first stage booster, designated B1063, executed its main engine cutoff and stage separation about 2.5 minutes into flight, sending the second stage to continue onward to low Earth orbit (LEO). The vehicle's two-piece protective payload fairing was jettisoned just before T+3 minutes. A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket launches 27 Starlink satellites from California on Oct. 23, 2026.
